question.text: What is a key drawback of relying on real estate as a retirement income asset?

answer.text: It cannot generate any rental income for retirees
It always loses value over long holding periods
Low liquidity and ongoing maintenance/management costs
It is exempt from all property-related taxes for retirees

explanation.text: The Logic: Real estate held for retirement income suffers from two structural drawbacks: it is illiquid (units are large and indivisible, and selling typically takes weeks or months and incurs transaction friction), and it requires ongoing maintenance, repair and management costs (society dues, repairs, property tax, tenant management). These features make it harder to use real estate to meet sudden cash needs in retirement and lower the effective net yield from rental income. The Trap: "Cannot generate rental income" is incorrect — rental income is one of the main reasons retirees hold real estate. "Always loses value over long holding periods" overstates risk; real estate values are cyclical, not monotonically declining. "Exempt from all property-related taxes" is factually wrong; retirees remain subject to property tax, applicable rental income tax and capital gains tax. Note: The cited NISM Series XVII Retirement Adviser workbook pages discuss real estate as an investment, rental income, maintenance and downsizing, and identify low liquidity and ongoing costs as concerns. The framing above is consistent with that general discussion and does not rely on any specific rent-versus-own housing-cost certainty claim.
